I'm noting the last close values—S&P 7422.1, Composite 24561.7—and checking that the Composite's shape-matching against 1998 aligns well with the NDX result. Looking at the S&P's ten historical analogs, the median returns skew negative (−1.5% at 1m, −2.6% at 3m, −3.1% at 6m), with only 30-40% of cases showing gains.

Comparing this against unconditional base rates shows a much more bullish picture—3m median +2.7% (67% up), 6m +5.2% (71% up)—and a simple pullback-based state ("4-7% below a recent high") gives even better odds, 75% up at 3m with +4.8% median. So the shape-analog model and the simple base-rate model clash directly, though both samples are thin.

For the Nasdaq Composite, the shape analogs (best match being October 1998's explosive +46% three-month run) suggest median gains of +5.4% at 3m and +8.5% at 6m with 60% up, while the Composite's state base rate shows +10.5% at 6m with 76% up but a typical −7.3% drawdown first. This creates an odd tension: the S&P pattern resembles a post-top 2000 scenario (more downside ahead) while the Nasdaq pattern resembles pre-blow-off 1998 (upside ahead)—and historically these can't coexist, since the 2000 S&P peak actually followed the 1998-99 Nasdaq blow-off.

Things to watch: whether 10-year yields push past 5%, Nasdaq vs S&P leadership, breadth, and whether S&P holds around −10% (near 7,040), echoing how the 2000 pullback first bottomed near −11% in mid-April.

For the chart, I'm plotting an S&P fan with median, p25, p75, the rebased 2000 path from May 4, and today's level—five series total, with x-axis labels approximating calendar dates.

I also need a Nasdaq fan overlaying the 1998 path from October 19, so I'll fetch those small historical ranges and pass the fan arrays as parameters to avoid recomputing them. Then I'll append section 8 to the report, include the analog table, and commit everything.
